prompt: What makes an interface a functional interface?

choices.text: The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation on it
choices.why: The annotation only asks the compiler to check; an interface without it can still qualify.

choices.text: Exactly one abstract method
choices.why: Right. That is the whole definition.

choices.text: Living in the package `java.util.function`
choices.why: `Comparator`, `Runnable` and your own `PriceRule` qualify from elsewhere.

choices.text: Having no default or static methods at all
choices.why: Those are allowed; `Comparator` has more than a dozen.

prompt: Somebody adds `String label();` to an interface that many lambdas implement. With `@FunctionalInterface` on it, what changes?

choices.text: Nothing: the lambdas still compile, and `label` returns `null`
choices.why: A lambda can only fill one method; the code stops compiling.

choices.text: An error appears at the interface itself, as well as at each lambda
choices.why: Right. The annotation puts the error where the mistake was made.

choices.text: The compiler generates a default body for `label`
choices.why: It never invents bodies.

choices.text: Only the lambdas fail, and the interface compiles
choices.why: That is what happens without the annotation.

prompt: Which of these, added to an interface with one abstract method, keep it functional? Choose all that apply.
hint: Only abstract methods that need a body from the lambda count.

choices.text: `default String describe() { ... }`
choices.why: Yes: it has a body.

choices.text: `static PriceRule none() { ... }`
choices.why: Yes: it belongs to the interface.

choices.text: `boolean equals(Object o);`
choices.why: Yes: every object already has a body for it.

choices.text: `String label();`
choices.why: No: a second abstract method.

prompt: Match each interface with its method.
`list.removeIf(...)` asks for one of the four. Which, and what will it do with your lambda?
hint: It has to decide, for each element, whether to remove it.

choices.text: A `Function`, to turn each element into its replacement
choices.why: Nothing is replaced; elements are kept or removed.

choices.text: A `Consumer`, to hand it each element as it is removed
choices.why: A consumer returns nothing, so it could not say which to remove.

choices.text: A `Predicate`, to test each element
choices.why: Right. `true` removes it.

choices.text: A `Supplier`, to provide the elements to remove
choices.why: The list already has the elements; nothing needs supplying.

prompt: `newShelf.get()` was called twice and printed one full list and one empty one. What does that show?

choices.text: Each call runs the body again and builds a new list
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: The second call cleared the list the first one filled
choices.why: The first list still printed full; nothing cleared it.

choices.text: A `Supplier` keeps the value it returned and copies it
choices.why: It keeps nothing; it runs its body on each call.

choices.text: The `ArrayList` was garbage-collected between calls
choices.why: It was still referenced by `shelf`, and printed.

prompt: A `Function<T, T>` whose input and output have the same type has its own name: `___<T>`.

choices.text: An `int` in, a `String` out
choices.why: That would be `IntFunction<String>`.

choices.text: A `String` in, an `int` out
choices.why: Right, with `applyAsInt`.

choices.text: A `String` in, an `Integer` object out
choices.why: The point of the family is that the `int` is never boxed.

choices.text: Two `int` values in, a `String` out
choices.why: Two inputs would say `Bi` in the name.

prompt: Why does `IntPredicate` exist when `Predicate<Integer>` already tests numbers?
hint: What a type argument must be.

choices.text: `Predicate<Integer>` cannot test negative numbers
choices.why: It tests any `Integer`.

choices.text: `IntPredicate` runs on several processors
choices.why: Nothing about it is parallel.

choices.text: It takes an `int` without boxing it into an object
choices.why: Right. Generics need objects, so `Predicate<Integer>` boxes each number.

choices.text: Older code used it before generics were added in Java 5
choices.why: It arrived in Java 8, with lambdas.

prompt: How many interfaces did `ListFunctions.java` find in `java.util.function`?
`Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000;` and `a == b` printed `false`. Why?

choices.text: The two numbers were rounded differently
choices.why: Integers are exact.

choices.text: They are two objects, and `==` compares references
choices.why: Right. Boxing made two `Integer` objects.

choices.text: 1000 does not fit in an `Integer`
choices.why: It fits easily.

choices.text: `==` is undefined for wrapper types and answers at random
choices.why: It is defined: it compares references, and the answer is repeatable.

prompt: `Function<Path, String> read = p -> Files.readString(p);` fails with `unreported exception IOException`. Why does a `throws` on `main` not fix it?
hint: Whose method is the lambda's body?

choices.text: `main` is not allowed to throw checked exceptions
choices.why: It can; `OwnInterface.java`'s `main` does.

choices.text: The body is `apply`, which declares no exceptions
choices.why: Right. It runs whenever `apply` is called, not inside `main`.

choices.text: `IOException` cannot be thrown from any lambda
choices.why: It can, from a lambda whose interface declares it.

choices.text: `Files.readString` is not allowed inside a lambda
choices.why: Any method may be called; the problem is the exception.

prompt: A colleague's bridge catches the `IOException` and returns an empty string. What does the lesson say is wrong with it?

choices.text: It is slower than throwing
choices.why: Speed is not the objection.

choices.text: Empty strings cannot be returned from a `Function`
choices.why: They can; that is the danger.

choices.text: A missing file then reads as an empty one, silently
choices.why: Right. `UncheckedIOException` keeps the failure and its cause.

choices.text: The compiler rejects a `catch` inside a lambda
choices.why: `unchecked` has one, and compiles.

hint: The table at the end of section 05.

pairs.left: The shape exists and nothing throws
The body throws a checked exception

prompt: A method takes a `Supplier<Report>` instead of a `Report`. Which reason from this lesson fits best?
hint: Nothing is built until somebody asks.

choices.text: A `Supplier` lets the method change the report
choices.why: It could change a `Report` it was given just as well.

choices.text: Building the report is slow, and not every call needs one
choices.why: Right. The method calls `get` only if it needs one.

choices.text: A `Supplier` is smaller in memory than the object
choices.why: Size is not the reason given.

choices.text: `Report` is a checked exception
choices.why: Nothing suggests that.
